questions.q: What kind of marine mammal was the gangchi that once lived on Dokdo?

wrong.2: Both are in the flipper-footed sea mammal group, but they are different species. This was the most common wrong answer.

questions.q: How often do Dokdo's guards change teams?
questions.fact: Dokdo's guard teams change about every [[2 months]].
questions.explain: Even with little space and rough waves, the guards keep a tight watch 24 hours a day.
questions.tip: Give the guards credit for their hard work in tough conditions.
questions.deep: About 40 members of the Dokdo Guard serve under the Gyeongsangbuk-do Provincial Police Agency. They switch teams every 2 months. The key point is that police, not soldiers, guard Dokdo. An area in dispute would have soldiers. But Dokdo is an ordinary part of the Republic of Korea where the police keep order, so police are stationed there.

wrong.0: You may be thinking of how often supply boats run.

questions.q: What did Choi Jong-deok build to reach Mulgol, Seodo's water source?
choices: A rope ladder on the cliff
questions.fact: Choi Jong-deok built [[998]] cement steps to reach Mulgol.

questions.tip: A moving story about the effort behind everyday life on Dokdo.

questions.q: What happens if you send a letter to Dokdo?

It is delivered only as far as Ulleungdo

questions.fact: Dokdo has a mailbox, and letters [[are delivered]].

questions.tip: The best quiz for showing sovereignty in everyday life.

questions.q: According to this source, when did Japan begin the school teaching about Dokdo described here?

questions.q: When did LTE mobile service first open on Dokdo?

questions.tip: Compare its date with Isabu's expedition in 512: more than 1,100 years apart.

questions.q: What is the largest vessel class that Dokdo's docking facility can accommodate?
questions.fact: Dokdo's docking facility can accommodate vessels up to the [[500-ton class]].

questions.tip: The larger ship classes are plausible distractions.

questions.q: How does Dokdo's evergreen spindle grow differently from the same species inland?
choices: Its branches spread close to the ground in strong sea winds
It grows faster by absorbing seawater
It reproduces only by roots and never flowers
It sheds leaves in winter to conserve water

questions.tip: Its shape offers a memorable image of endurance.

questions.q: Which well-known plant grows purple flowers in cracks in Dokdo's rocks?
questions.fact: The [[seashore aster]] is a well-known plant that grows purple flowers in cracks in Dokdo's rocks.

questions.q: What name for Dokdo appears in Japan's 1870 report on relations with Joseon?

A section addressed how Ulleungdo and Dokdo became dependencies of Joseon, using the contemporary Japanese names Takeshima and Matsushima. The source emphasizes that this Japanese government record predates the claimed incorporation of 1905 by 35 years.

questions.q: When is Dokdo Day?
questions.fact: Dokdo Day is [[October 25]].
questions.explain: Dokdo Day marks October 25, 1900. On that day, Emperor Gojong issued Imperial Edict No. 41 of the Korean Empire, officially making Dokdo part of Ulleung County.
questions.tip: A symbolic question for the 100th-episode special. Keep it light.

questions.q: Which sea is Dokdo in?
questions.fact: Dokdo is Korean land in [[the East Sea]].
questions.explain: Dokdo is the island farthest east in Korea. It is the first place in Korea to see the sunrise.
questions.tip: Start here: this is the most basic question.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which bird is seen most often on Dokdo?
questions.fact: The bird seen most often on Dokdo is the [[black-tailed gull]].
questions.explain: The black-tailed gull gets its Korean name from its cat-like cry. It is known as an old-timer on Dokdo.
questions.tip: Tell kids about its cat-like cry. They love it.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How many large islands make up Dokdo?
questions.fact: Dokdo is made up of [[2]] large islands and smaller rocky islands.
questions.explain: The two large islands are Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet). Small rocky islands lie around them.
questions.tip: Students learn the names Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet) in the next grade.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What shines a light out to sea from Dokdo at night?
questions.fact: Dokdo has a [[lighthouse]] that lights up the sea at night.
questions.explain: Dokdo Lighthouse stands on top of Dongdo (East Islet). It helps passing ships find their way.
questions.tip: The lighthouse story ties in with the light-up map.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What do you ride to get to Dokdo?
questions.fact: People travel to Dokdo by [[boat]].
questions.explain: You take a boat from Ulleungdo. On days with high waves, boats may not sail, so visitors may have to turn back.
questions.tip: A natural way to explain why sailings get canceled.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What are the names of Dokdo's two large islands?
questions.fact: Dokdo's two large islands are [[Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet)]].
questions.explain: Dongdo (East Islet) gets its name from being on the east side. Seodo (West Islet) gets its name from being on the west side. The sea between them is very shallow.
questions.tip: Their names match their directions, so they're easy to remember.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which island is Dokdo's lighthouse on?
questions.fact: Dokdo's lighthouse is on [[Dongdo (East Islet)]].
questions.explain: The guards' rooms are also on Dongdo (East Islet). So are the helicopter landing pad and the boat dock.
questions.tip: People come and go on Dongdo (East Islet); Seodo (West Islet) has a water source.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which is the only bird that lives on Dokdo all year?
questions.fact: The only bird that lives on Dokdo all year is the [[sparrow]].
questions.explain: Other birds come and go with the seasons. Sparrows stay on Dokdo all year.
questions.tip: People are often surprised that sparrows live on Dokdo, too.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which province is Dokdo part of?
questions.fact: Dokdo is part of Ulleung County in [[Gyeongsangbuk-do]].
questions.explain: Dokdo's address is Dokdo-ri, Ulleung-eup, Ulleung-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do.
questions.tip: Having a Korean address is itself evidence that Dokdo is Korean territory.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How was Dokdo formed?
questions.fact: Dokdo was formed when [[an underwater volcano rose up]].
questions.explain: Dokdo is the top of a huge volcano that rose from 2,000 m below the sea.
questions.tip: It's the older sibling: Dokdo formed before Ulleungdo.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: When do black-tailed gulls lay eggs and raise chicks on Dokdo?
questions.fact: Black-tailed gulls raise their chicks on Dokdo [[from spring to summer]].
questions.explain: From late March to July, Dokdo becomes a giant nursery for black-tailed gulls.
questions.tip: Photos from this season show Dokdo blanketed in white birds.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What is the name of the highest peak on Dokdo's Dongdo (East Islet)?
questions.fact: The highest peak on Dokdo's Dongdo (East Islet) is [[Usanbong]].
questions.explain: Daehanbong is the highest point on Seodo (West Islet). Usanbong is the highest point on Dongdo (East Islet).
questions.tip: The name comes from Usando, an old name for Dokdo.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How high is Dokdo's highest point?
questions.fact: Dokdo's highest point is Daehanbong on Seodo (West Islet), at about [[168 m]].
questions.explain: Usanbong on Dongdo (East Islet) is 98.6 m high, while Daehanbong on Seodo (West Islet) is 168.5 m. Seodo is much higher and steeper.
questions.tip: Think of roughly a 50-story apartment building.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How far can Dokdo Lighthouse's light reach?
questions.fact: Dokdo Lighthouse's light reaches about [[25 nautical miles]].
questions.explain: Its light can be seen from about 46 km away at sea.
questions.tip: In the dark East Sea, the light marks the island.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How do people on Dokdo obtain drinking water?
choices: By turning seawater into fresh water
By digging deep into the ground
questions.fact: Dokdo obtains water using equipment that [[turns seawater into fresh water]].
questions.explain: The source gives production as 27 tons a day. Seodo (West Islet) also has a natural spring called Mulgol.
questions.tip: This connects daily life with the question of an island's ability to sustain habitation.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which bird of prey raises its young on the high cliffs of Seodo (West Islet)?
questions.fact: [[Falcons]] raise their young on the cliffs of Seodo (West Islet).
questions.explain: Cliffs that are difficult for people to climb provide safe nesting places for falcons.
questions.tip: Contrast Dongdo's facilities with Seodo's birds and trees.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: In which year was Dokdo Lighthouse first lit?
questions.fact: Dokdo Lighthouse was first lit in [[1954]].
questions.explain: The lighthouse first shone in August 1954, nine years after Korea's liberation.
questions.tip: This was during the Dokdo Volunteer Garrison's activity.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which is Dokdo's administrative address?
questions.fact: Dokdo's address is [[Dokdo-ri, Ulleung-eup, Ulleung-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do]].
questions.explain: It has a formal address, including lot numbers. Letters are delivered using postal code 40240.
questions.tip: Connect the administrative address, postal code and road names.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: In which year was Dokdo's docking facility built?
questions.fact: Dokdo's docking facility was built in [[1997]].
questions.explain: The 80 m facility on Dongdo (East Islet) enabled vessels of up to the 500-ton class to dock.
questions.tip: The facility helped make public visits possible.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: About how many bird species are reported in the source as observed on Dokdo?
questions.fact: The source reports about [[80]] bird species observed on Dokdo.
questions.explain: Despite its small size, Dokdo lies on a migration route. The text reports more than 15,000 visiting birds each year.
questions.tip: A small island can support a large ecological story.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: In which year was an internet satellite antenna installed on Dokdo?
questions.fact: An internet satellite antenna was installed on Dokdo in [[2000]].
questions.explain: Satellite internet in 2000 and LTE in 2013 connected the island more closely with the mainland.
questions.tip: A timeline of infrastructure and modern administration.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which tree on Dokdo, more than 100 years old, became a Natural Monument?
questions.fact: Dokdo's tree older than 100 years and designated a Natural Monument is an [[evergreen spindle]].
questions.explain: Strong sea winds keep it close to the ground, but it has endured for more than a century.
questions.tip: Its endurance makes a memorable image.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Area: Dongdo (East Islet) 73,297 m²; Seodo (West Islet) 88,740 m²; smaller islands 25,517 m²; total 187,554 m².

Subtract the smaller islands from the total. What is the combined area of the two main islets?
questions.fact: Subtracting 25,517 m² from 187,554 m² gives a combined main-islet area of [[162,037 m²]].
questions.explain: Subtract the smaller islands: 187,554 - 25,517 = 162,037 m². Adding the two main islets gives the same result.
questions.deep: The total consists of Dongdo, Seodo and the smaller islands. First distinguish the whole from the part being asked for. This is an aggregation of the supplied land areas; it does not add the sea shown on a map or the channel between the islets.

wrong.1: This total still includes the smaller islands.
wrong.2: This is the difference between the two main-islet areas.
wrong.3: This is the area to be excluded.

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Dongdo (East Islet): 73,297 m². Total Dokdo land area: 187,554 m².

What percentage of the total is Dongdo, rounded to one decimal place for a pie chart?
questions.fact: Dongdo's 73,297 m² as a percentage of 187,554 m² rounds to [[39.1%]].
questions.explain: Divide Dongdo's area by the total and multiply by 100. About 39.08% rounds to 39.1%.
questions.deep: Define the whole before calculating a percentage. The denominator here is all of Dokdo, including the smaller islands, not just the two main islets. Keep sufficient decimal places during the division and round only at the end.

wrong.0: This is Seodo's share of the total.
wrong.2: This is the smaller islands' share.
wrong.3: This combines Dongdo and Seodo.

[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Heights: Dongdo (East Islet) 98.6 m, Seodo (West Islet) 168.5 m. Coastlines: Dongdo 2.8 km, Seodo 2.6 km.

What is the difference between the two stated heights?
questions.fact: The difference between 168.5 m and 98.6 m is [[69.9 m]].
questions.explain: Use the height measurements in meters: 168.5 - 98.6 = 69.9 m. Do not use the coastline figures in kilometers.
questions.deep: Area, height and coastline length may appear in one table, but they are not interchangeable. Select the same measurement for both islets before finding a difference. This result is not the full height of a particular cliff or the depth of the channel.

wrong.1: This misuses the coastline difference as a height difference.
wrong.3: The result must remain in meters, not kilometers.

[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Dongdo (East Islet): 73,297 m², coastline 2.8 km. Seodo (West Islet): 88,740 m², coastline 2.6 km.

Compare coastline per 10,000 m² using (coastline in m / area in m²) x 10,000. Which result is correct?
questions.fact: Comparing coastline per 10,000 m² gives [[a longer value for Dongdo]].
questions.explain: Convert coastline lengths to meters. Dongdo has about 382 m per 10,000 m², compared with about 293 m for Seodo.
questions.deep: Using the same area denominator makes differently sized islands comparable. This is only an indicator calculated from the table. It cannot by itself determine the difficulty of field surveys or the ecological value of either islet.

wrong.0: A larger area does not by itself mean a longer coastline per unit area.
wrong.1: The results differ: about 382 m versus 293 m.
wrong.2: After converting km to m, the supplied formula allows comparison.

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Dongdo (East Islet): 73,297 m², coastline 2.8 km. Seodo (West Islet): 88,740 m², coastline 2.6 km.

A caption says, "Of these two islets, the one with the larger area also has the longer coastline." How does the table test that claim?
questions.fact: Seodo's larger area but shorter coastline provides a [[counterexample]] to the claim.
questions.explain: Seodo has the larger area but a 2.6 km coastline, shorter than Dongdo's 2.8 km. The claim does not fit the table.
questions.deep: Do not assume two different measurements always move in the same direction. Check the objects and conditions in a claim, then look for a case that meets those conditions but contradicts its conclusion. That is the counterexample sought here.

wrong.1: Seodo is larger in area but shorter in coastline.
wrong.2: Height is not the coastline measure in the claim.
wrong.3: The coastlines are 2.8 km and 2.6 km, not equal.

questions.fact: Applying both changes in Article 1 gives [[Uldo / county magistrate]].

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 2 places the county office in Taeha-dong and gives it jurisdiction over all Ulleungdo, Jukdo and Seokdo.

A draft says "Office location: all Ulleungdo, Jukdo and Seokdo / Jurisdiction: Taeha-dong." How should it be corrected?
questions.fact: The draft reverses office location and jurisdiction, so the correction is [[to exchange the two fields' contents]].
questions.distractor: to change only the office location
blankDistractors: to change only the office location
questions.explain: The location and the area of jurisdiction have been reversed. Exchanging them brings both fields into line with Article 2.
questions.deep: Where an institution is located and the area it administers are different kinds of information. Mixing them merely because both contain place names changes the meaning of an administrative record. Both fields need checking, not just one.

wrong.0: The jurisdiction would still incorrectly be Taeha-dong.
wrong.1: The office location would still be a list of islands.
wrong.3: The office location and jurisdiction are reversed.

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 4 gives priority to taxes collected on the island to fund initial expenses.

[Hypothetical budget] Expenses are 100 nyang, and 40 nyang of island taxes are available. After applying that 40 nyang, what shortfall remains?
questions.fact: In the hypothetical budget, 100 nyang of expenses minus 40 nyang of revenue leaves [[60 nyang]].
questions.explain: Subtract the available funding from the need: 100 - 40 = 60 nyang. These amounts are hypothetical, not historical statistics.
questions.deep: Article 4 states a funding priority; it does not supply the budget amounts used in this exercise. Distinguish the documented funding principle from the author's calculation assumptions. This extract does not tell us how much was obtained from other sources.

wrong.0: This is the funding already applied, not the shortfall.
wrong.1: This is the original total need.
wrong.2: Adding need and revenue does not give a shortfall.

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 5 provides for later supplementation of incomplete rules. Article 6 makes the edict effective from promulgation.

An editor writes, "The edict does not take effect until every incomplete rule is supplemented." What correction applies both articles?
choices: Delay commencement until all rules are complete
Delete supplementation because the edict is already effective
questions.fact: Reading Articles 5 and 6 together requires [[separating commencement from supplementation]].
questions.distractor: delaying commencement until supplementation is complete
blankDistractors: delaying commencement until supplementation is complete
Treat enforcement and later revision as identical
questions.explain: Article 5 concerns later additions, while Article 6 fixes commencement. Neither says that unfinished details postpone commencement.
questions.deep: Identify what each provision governs. An immediate effective date and later additions to detailed rules can coexist. Adding a postponement condition that the text does not contain changes the source.

wrong.1: This changes Article 6's effective-date rule.
wrong.2: Immediate effect and later supplementation can coexist.
wrong.3: The provision directly governing commencement cannot be ignored.

[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 1: Gangwon-do affiliation and magistrate title. Article 2: Taeha-dong office and jurisdiction over Ulleungdo, Jukdo and Seokdo. Article 4: initial expenses funded first from taxes.

Match A=province and title, B=office location and jurisdiction, C=initial funding. Which articles match A, B and C in order?
questions.fact: The article order for organization, location/jurisdiction and initial funding is [[1 / 2 / 4]].
questions.explain: Match each check to its topic: Article 1 for organization, Article 2 for location and jurisdiction, and Article 4 for initial funding.
questions.deep: Citing a source does not mean every statement is supported by every part of it. Link each item under review to the provision that directly supports it. This is practice in matching separate claims to their evidence.

wrong.0: The articles for A and B are reversed.
wrong.2: The articles for B and C are reversed.
wrong.3: The articles for A and C are reversed.

[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
Isotakeshima means Ulleungdo; Matsushima means Dokdo. Fukuura is a place on Dogo in the Oki Islands.

Convert "Fukuura -> Matsushima -> Isotakeshima" into modern island names, starting with the island group containing the departure point.
questions.fact: The modern-name sequence is [[Oki Islands / Dokdo / Ulleungdo]].
blankDistractors: Ulleungdo, Dokdo and the Oki Islands
Dokdo, the Oki Islands and Ulleungdo
questions.explain: Use the supplied name equivalents: Fukuura is in Oki, Matsushima is Dokdo, and Isotakeshima is Ulleungdo.
questions.deep: Historical place names do not necessarily match present usage. This exercise uses the identifications in the commentary for one particular map. It does not authorize applying the same name table to every map from every period without checking.

wrong.0: The names for the two islands are reversed.
wrong.1: The departure point and final destination are reversed.
wrong.3: This incorrectly places Fukuura on Dokdo.

[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
Recorded distances: Dokdo to Ulleungdo about 40 ri; Fukuura to Dokdo about 80 ri. These are historical map figures, not modern measurements.

What is the simplest whole-number ratio of the two recorded distances, in that order?
questions.fact: The ratio of 40 ri to 80 ri is [[1:2]].
questions.explain: Both values use the same unit. Divide both parts of 40:80 by 40 to obtain 1:2.
questions.deep: Follow the order requested when calculating a ratio. The result compares figures recorded on an old map. It does not mean modern route lengths or sailing times have the same ratio.

wrong.0: This reverses the requested order.
wrong.1: This uses the sum of the distances as the second value.
wrong.2: The recorded distances are not equal.

[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
The recorded Dokdo-to-Ulleungdo distance is about 40 ri. The commentary uses 1 ri as approximately 3.9 km.

Convert the historical figure, not the modern measured distance. What is about 40 ri using this conversion?
questions.fact: Converting 40 ri at about 3.9 km per ri gives about [[156 km]].
questions.explain: 40 x 3.9 = 156 km. This converts the old map's figure; it is not the modern measured distance between the islands.
questions.deep: Converting an old unit and testing the accuracy of an old record are different tasks. A unit conversion does not remove errors in the original measurement. Label the result as a conversion of the historical figure.

wrong.1: This loses one decimal place in multiplication.
wrong.2: This converts 80 ri instead.
wrong.3: This divides 40 by 3.9 instead of multiplying.

[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
Recorded segments: Fukuura to Dokdo about 80 ri; Dokdo to Ulleungdo about 40 ri. These are historical map values.

Add the two consecutive segments. What total is recorded for the route?
questions.fact: Adding the historical segments of 80 ri and 40 ri gives about [[120 ri]].
questions.explain: 80 + 40 = 120 ri. A two-segment route is different from the straight-line distance between its endpoints.
questions.deep: A route through several segments has the sum of their lengths. This is not necessarily the direct distance between the start and finish. The exercise calculates old recorded values; it does not reconstruct an actual sailing route.

wrong.2: This uses only the longer segment.

From Dokdo, Ulleungdo is to the northwest.

Reverse the reference point: from Ulleungdo, in which direction is Dokdo?
questions.fact: Reversing the stated northwest relation places Dokdo [[southeast]] of Ulleungdo.
questions.explain: Reversing the endpoints changes north to south and west to east. The opposite of northwest is southeast.
questions.deep: A direction depends on the reference point. Reusing the original direction after exchanging the start and destination reverses their relation incorrectly. This reads a compass relationship from the commentary, not an actual navigational bearing.

wrong.0: This keeps the original direction despite changing the reference point.
wrong.1: The north-south component has not been reversed.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Articles 3 and 57: territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles and EEZ outer limit up to 200 nautical miles, both measured from the same baseline.
[Assumption] Ignore overlapping national claims; this does not determine actual boundaries around Dokdo.

An officer adds 200 miles beyond a 12-mile territorial sea. At what distance from the baseline should the EEZ limit instead be drawn?
questions.fact: The EEZ maximum is measured from the same baseline at [[200 nautical miles]], without adding the 12-mile territorial sea.
questions.explain: Both limits are measured from the baseline. The EEZ maximum is not 200 miles beyond the territorial sea's outer edge.
questions.deep: Check the starting point before adding distances from different provisions. This is a hypothetical application of a general maximum. It does not determine actual delimitation or any particular island's maritime entitlement.

wrong.0: This counts the territorial-sea width twice.
wrong.1: The baseline, not the territorial-sea boundary, is the reference point.
wrong.2: This wrongly adds the contiguous-zone maximum.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Articles 3, 33 and 57: maxima from the same baseline are territorial sea 12, contiguous-zone outer limit 24 and EEZ outer limit 200 nautical miles.
[Assumption] Test only these distance ceilings, not actual delimitation.

Plans, in the order above: A=(10,24,190), B=(14,24,190), C=(10,26,190), D=(10,24,210). Which meets all three ceilings?
questions.fact: Of the four hypothetical plans, [[Plan A]] alone meets all three distance ceilings.
questions.explain: Only A stays within all three maxima. Meeting these distance limits does not mean that every other legal requirement is satisfied.
questions.deep: A maximum is a ceiling, not a value that must always be used. A 10-mile territorial sea or 190-mile EEZ limit is not excluded by these distance conditions alone. Overlap with other states is outside the assumptions.

wrong.1: A 14-mile territorial sea exceeds the 12-mile maximum.
wrong.2: A 26-mile contiguous-zone limit exceeds 24 miles.
wrong.3: A 210-mile EEZ limit exceeds 200 miles.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Articles 3, 33, 55 and 57: the contiguous zone and EEZ lie beyond the territorial sea. Their outer maxima are 24 and 200 nautical miles from the baseline.
[Assumption] No overlap with other states.

Set the territorial sea at 12 miles, contiguous-zone limit at 24 and EEZ limit at 200. Which two distance-based labels can apply together at 18 miles?
questions.fact: With the stated limits, a point 18 miles from the baseline can lie in both the [[contiguous zone and EEZ]].
questions.explain: 18 is beyond 12 but within both 24 and 200. The contiguous zone and EEZ can overlap spatially.
questions.deep: Maritime-zone names do not always denote mutually exclusive strips. Zones with different legal functions can occupy the same space. Spatial overlap does not make every power exercised there identical.

wrong.0: 18 miles is outside the stated territorial sea.
wrong.2: The point can be in the EEZ, but not the territorial sea.
wrong.3: The point is seaward of both the baseline and territorial-sea boundary.

[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Article 57: the EEZ outer limit cannot exceed 200 nautical miles from the baseline used to measure the territorial sea.

On a teaching scale, not an actual map, the baseline is at 0 cm and 1 cm represents 20 nautical miles. Where should the maximum be marked?
questions.fact: At 20 nautical miles per centimeter, the 200-mile maximum lies at [[10 cm]].
questions.explain: Divide 200 by 20: the mark lies 10 cm from zero.
questions.deep: Divide the total real distance by the distance represented by one centimeter. This teaching scale does not reproduce an actual coastline or baseline. Do not use the calculated position as a real maritime boundary around Dokdo.

wrong.0: This represents only 20 nautical miles.
wrong.1: This represents 100 nautical miles.
wrong.3: This represents 400 nautical miles, twice the maximum.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Article 33: in the contiguous zone, necessary control may prevent or punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration or sanitary laws within a state's territory or territorial sea.

[Assumption] A vessel is 18 miles from the baseline, beyond a 12-mile territorial sea. Which purpose directly supports action to prevent smuggling into the state?
questions.fact: The directly relevant Article 33 purpose is [[preventing customs-law infringements]].
blankDistractors: A change in the vessel's nationality
questions.explain: Article 33 permits necessary control to prevent customs-law infringements within the territory or territorial sea. It is not unlimited control over every activity.
questions.deep: Check the purpose and scope of a provision as well as the location. This asks whether the purpose of a measure matches the provision. It does not decide the legality of a particular coercive action against a specific vessel.

wrong.0: This wrongly converts limited control into a power of annexation.
wrong.1: This is not the control purpose stated in the article.
wrong.2: Necessary control is different from an unconditional blanket ban.

questions.q: Which document issued by the Meiji government's Foreign Ministry in 1870 described Ulleungdo and Dokdo as dependencies of Joseon?
questions.fact: The circumstances in which Ulleungdo and Dokdo became dependencies of Joseon appear in the 1870 [[Chosengoku Kosai Shimatsu Naitansho]].
questions.explain: The Meiji Foreign Ministry prepared this report in 1870. A separate heading describes how the two islands became dependencies of Joseon, seven years before the Dajokan Directive.
questions.deep: The document's title, Chosengoku Kosai Shimatsu Naitansho, means a confidential report on relations with Joseon. In 1870, soon after the Meiji government was established, the Foreign Ministry sent officials to investigate conditions in Joseon. The report includes a separate section on how Ulleungdo and Dokdo became dependencies of Joseon. The important point is that the heading itself treats the two islands as dependencies of Joseon. Japanese officials carried out the investigation and wrote the report. Its timing matters: seven years before the 1877 Dajokan Directive and 35 years before Japan's 1905 incorporation claim. Japan described Dokdo as ownerless in 1905, although its own Foreign Ministry had associated the island with Joseon a generation earlier. Question #099, on the same fact, had a correct-answer rate of only 20%. The Dajokan Directive is better known; this report is less familiar.

wrong.0: The Dajokan Directive dates to 1877, seven years later.
wrong.1: Onshu Shicho Goki is a Japanese geography book from 1667, over 200 years earlier.
wrong.3: Shimane Notice No. 40 claimed incorporation in 1905, a very different purpose.

questions.q: Which Japanese person was executed in 1837 after violating the ban on travel to Ulleungdo?
questions.fact: In 1837, Hachiemon received [[the death penalty]] for illegally traveling to Ulleungdo.
questions.explain: The ban first issued in 1696 remained in force. Hachiemon's execution shows that it was enforced, not merely written down.
questions.deep: Hachiemon was a merchant from Hamada in Iwami Province, now part of Shimane Prefecture. He went to Ulleungdo in 1836 to cut timber and trade. After discovery, he was tried and executed in 1837. The case is important for its attached map as well as its punishment. Japan is yellow; Joseon's Ulleungdo and Dokdo are red. The court records thus distinguish the islands visually. The source interprets the severe punishment as showing how seriously the shogunate treated the ban on crossing to these islands. The 1696 ban was still being enforced 141 years later. A qualification is essential: the charges concerned violation of the travel ban and illicit trade. The punishment alone does not settle sovereignty. It must be read with the map and the wider historical context.

questions.q: Who personally carved 'Korean Territory' into the rock on Dokdo's Dongdo (East Islet)?
questions.fact: In August 1953, [[Hong Sun-chil]] carved 'Korean Territory' into a rock on Dongdo (East Islet).
questions.explain: The source dates the carving to August 5, 1953. The three characters remain on the rock.
questions.deep: Hong Sun-chil came from Ulleungdo. In 1953, amid the aftermath of the Korean War, he organized 33 volunteers to defend Dokdo when the state's capacity to protect it was limited. On August 5, 1953, he carved 'Korean Territory' into a rock on Dongdo (East Islet). Rather than leaving a removable sign, he cut the declaration directly into stone. The volunteers later handed their duties to the police in 1956. Hong also raised money for weapons by trading squid. These were practical efforts by civilians to protect the island. Dokdo's road names honor Isabu and An Yong-bok. Hong's name is not a road name, but his inscription remains part of the island itself.

wrong.0: Isabu conquered Usan State in 512, roughly 1,400 years earlier.
wrong.1: An Yong-bok was active in the seventeenth century.
wrong.3: Choi began living on Dokdo in 1965, after the inscription was made.

questions.q: In which year did Japan's Dajokan issue its directive stating that Ulleungdo and Dokdo had nothing to do with Japan?
questions.fact: Japan's Dajokan issued the directive on Ulleungdo and Dokdo in [[1877]].
questions.explain: The Dajokan was Japan's highest decision-making authority. Its directive stated that Ulleungdo and Dokdo had nothing to do with Japan.
questions.deep: The Dajokan was the highest governing body of early Meiji Japan, comparable to the later cabinet. In March 1877 it directed that Ulleungdo and the other island had nothing to do with Japan. The attached map helps identify the other island as Dokdo. The inquiry arose during a land-registry survey. Shimane Prefecture asked the Home Ministry whether the islands should be included. The ministry investigated historical records and referred the question to the Dajokan. The directive came after that investigation, not from a private opinion. It is a record produced by Japan's own central government. In 1905, just 28 years later, Japan claimed to incorporate Dokdo as ownerless territory. The source contrasts that claim with the earlier directive and notes its absence from Japanese promotional accounts.

wrong.0: 1868 is the year of the Meiji Restoration, nine years earlier.
wrong.2: 1895 is associated with the end of the First Sino-Japanese War.
wrong.3: 1905 is the year Japan claimed to incorporate Dokdo.

questions.q: Who was Dokdo's first civilian resident?
questions.fact: Dokdo's first civilian resident, who settled there in 1965, was [[Choi Jong-deok]].
questions.explain: Choi Jong-deok settled on Seodo (West Islet) in 1965 and made a living gathering seafood.
questions.deep: Choi Jong-deok was a diver from Ulleungdo. In March 1965 he settled on Seodo (West Islet), gathering abalone, turban snails and sea cucumbers. He built 998 cement steps to reach the Mulgol water source. This was difficult physical work necessary for daily life, not simply a symbolic visit. His presence differed from that of the guards: he was a civilian earning a living on the island. Kim Sung-do and his wife later continued civilian residence there. The supplied source states that Kim Shin-yeol died in March 2026, leaving no permanent civilian residents, and contrasts this with 112 Japanese registrations of permanent domicile. These time-specific statements are retained as source claims and require editorial verification before publication.

wrong.0: Kim Sung-do continued civilian residence after Choi.
wrong.2: Hong led the volunteer garrison; the question asks about civilian settlement.
wrong.3: An was a seventeenth-century fisherman, not the modern resident described here.

questions.q: Which old name for Dokdo came from the many sea lions living there?
questions.fact: Dokdo's old name [[Gajido]] came from gaji-eo, an old term for sea lions.
questions.explain: Sea lions were once called gaji-eo. Their abundance gave the island the name Gajido.
questions.deep: The Annals of King Jeongjo record a governor's report referring to Gajido and four or five sea lions. The name preserves a link between the island and the animals living there. The names Keungajebawi and Jageungajebawi, the large and small gaje rocks, preserve the same association. Place names can carry traces of earlier ecology. Usando, Seokdo and Gajido belong to different historical contexts. They should not be treated as interchangeable labels without considering their sources and dates. The source states that the sea lion was classified as extinct by the IUCN in 1994. The animal disappeared, but its old name remains in Dokdo's place names.

wrong.0: Usando is a name found in official historical records, not one derived from sea lions.
wrong.1: Sambongdo refers to three peaks.
wrong.3: Seokdo means stone island.

questions.fact: Shimane Prefecture established its so-called 'Takeshima Day' in [[2005]].
questions.explain: The prefecture chose February 22, marking the centenary of its 1905 incorporation notice.
questions.deep:
The date February 22 refers to Shimane Notice No. 40 of 1905. A century later, in 2005, Shimane Prefecture established the observance through a local ordinance.

Although it began as a prefectural event, senior officials from Japan's central government have attended. The source interprets this as giving national support to the territorial claim.

It also connects the event with repeated proposals for an ICJ referral: both are presented as ways to make Dokdo appear internationally disputed.

Korea's Dokdo Day is October 25, recalling Imperial Edict No. 41 of 1900. The source emphasizes the contrast with the Japanese notice issued five years later.

wrong.0: 1995 was ten years before the ordinance.
wrong.1: 2000 was five years before the ordinance.
wrong.3: 2010 was five years after the ordinance.

questions.q: In which year was the Dokdo Volunteer Garrison formed?
questions.fact: Hong Sun-chil and 33 young volunteers formed the Dokdo Volunteer Garrison in [[1953]].
questions.explain: The garrison was formed in 1953, during the Korean War period, to defend Dokdo.
questions.deep:
In the confusion surrounding the Korean War and armistice, Japanese patrol vessels approached Dokdo and territorial markers appeared. Hong Sun-chil and fellow islanders organized a civilian defense force.

Hong used money from his grandfather and profits from squid trading to buy equipment in Busan and Daegu, including M1 rifles and a mortar. Their resources did not simply arrive as government aid.

They also painted logs black to resemble large guns. The source says a Japanese magazine reported these as artillery and that aircraft approaches decreased. This is the story behind the garrison's well-known deception.

In 1956, the volunteers handed their duties to the national police. Civilian defense was followed by regular state policing.

wrong.0: 1948 predates the garrison's formation.
